div.p: This paper describes certain aspects of an architecture description language (MetaH) and associated toolset used to specify, analyze, and automatically assemble software for real-time, faulttolerant, secure, multi-processor systems. One goal in the design of this language and toolset was to provide design-time analysis that accurately characterizes the behavior of the actual implementation. Currently, our toolset consists of tools to automatically assemble the application software and to perform a real-time schedulability analysis for that application.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: We have recently completed a prototype toolset and architecture description language that allows specification, schedulability analysis, and automated code assembly for real-time applications. The language, called MetaH, allows a specification at a software architectural level rather than at a functional (source code) level [l, 3, 131. MetaH specifications identify modules written in Ada that are to be included and specify how those modules are to communicate, share resources, and be scheduled. The MetaH language serves as both a real-time modeling language and a design or architecture specification language for an application.

The MetaH toolset currently consists of a code generator and assembler, an application builder, a timing analyzer tool (real-time modeler and schedulability analyzer), and a graphical editor. The design of the real-time aspects of the sys-Pam Binns* Honeywell Technology Center Minneapolis, Minnesota 55418 binns@src. honeywell.com tem is based on rate monotonic scheduling theory [7], and emphasis has been placed on insuring that the assembled application is accurately described by the generated red-time model. The goal has been to achieve very high assurance that the results of the schedulability analysis in fact capture the real-time behavior of the application. This illustrates a fundamental theme of our overall approach: automatic code assembly and analysis driven from a common specification language, based on relevant underlying formal models.

We will first briefly outline the MetaH language itself. We will then focus on the generation of real-time process dispatching and inter-process communication code, and on the red-time model generated and schedulability analysis performed for these aspects of an application.

div.head: MetaH Language
div.p: At first glance, MetaH is similar to many existing structured design or object-oriented design notations. The graphical representation of MetaH al- lows entities to be placed on a screen and connected together, where each entity may be defined as another collection of connected entities in a hierarchical manner, as in Figure 1. However, MetaH has a rich set of entity types and detailed semantics, extensive and precise enough to perform a detailed real-time schedulability analysis and to automatically assemble a load image.

MetaH allows a specification of system components and connections, and attributes of those components and connections that are relevant to real-time, fault-tolerant, secure, and multiprocessor aspects of an application. The kinds of entities in a MetaH specification can be divided into lower-level entities that describe source code Figure 1: Example Graphical MetaH modules (e.g. subprograms, packages) or hardware elements (e.g. memories, processors); and higher-level entities that specify how previously declared entities may be combined to form new enti ties (modes, macros, systems, applications).

The language has both a textual and a graphical syntax defined, and tool support that will allow a MetaH specification to be viewed and edited interchangeably in either format is in progress. Figure 2 illustrates the general structure of MetaH specifications using the textual syntax. Figure 1 shows the graphic representation for the mode M interface (on the left) and the implementation M.EXAMPLE (on the right).

Entities have separate interface and implementation specifications, where multiple implementations can be specified for a given interface. An interface specification (e.g. mode M in Figure 2 and the left screen in Figure 1) may contain declarations of shareable monitors and packages; and/or source entities called ports and events (e.g. mode M has one port in its interface). An entity implementation may contain declarations for component entities and connections between those components (e.g. P1 and P2 are components within mode implementation M.EXAMPLE). In the graphical representation, the interface corresponds to the icon t o which it is connected (e.g. mode M on the left of Figure l), while an implementation corresponds to a diagram that shows one possible set of internal components and connections (e.g. the right screen of Figure 1 is an implementation for the mode M interface shown on the left).
In this paper, we will focus our attention on the semantics of periodic processes and on the connections between ports declared in the interfaces of periodic processes.

A process is the fundamental unit of scheduling, allocation to hardware processors, and fault and security containment. Process implementations identify source code modules and can specify a variety of attributes relating to real-time scheduling, security, fault behavior, and multiprocessor allocation. Both periodic and aperiodic processes are supported. While a periodic process is active it is automatically and repeatedly dispatched with some periodicity that is specified as an attribute of that process. All dispatched but not yet completed processes are scheduled according to a preemptive fixed priority discipline.

A process interface may (among other things) identify input and output ports, which correspond to input and output buffer variables within the source code. Process ports are connected together to indicate communication that is to occur between processes at run-time (e.g. between P1 and P2 in Figures 1 and2). Ports are strongly typed using the type system of the underlying source language, and port-to-port connections are type checked. Port-to-port connections cause periodic assignments to occur between the buffer variables associated with the ports declared in the process interfaces. These assignments must be scheduled t o occur in a way that takes into account the periodicities and deadlines of the communicating processes; this will be discussed shortly. The elements that form the application load image that is automatically produced from a MetaH specification are illustrated in Figure 3. The application source modules identified in the MetaH specification as part of each process are collected together and compiled and linked into separate process address spaces. The execution of these processes is managed by a customized executive, which consists of packages that are automatically generated from the MetaH specification to- gether with standard and target-dependent packages identified in the hardware architecture portions of the specification. The current version is targeted to a modified Tartan Ada multiple application run-time executing on a uni-processor i80960MC.

The generated executive packages constitute application-specific "glue" code that performs process dispatching, communication, event vectoring, mode changing, capability checking, and access synchronization for shared monitors. Generated tables contain data that control process scheduling, capabilities, etc. There is also a generated package in each application process that maps between the source identifiers used within that process and the global enumerations generated in the executive code. In the final load image, each process and the executive has its own protected address space, where the executive address space allows access to all process port buffer variables.

The scheduling of periodic activities, which includes periodic process dispatching and port-toport communication between periodic processes, is driven by a periodic hardware clock interrupt. At each interrupt a cycle counter is incremented by 1 (modulo some large value to avoid overflow), with the periodic scheduling actions that are to occur at an interrupt determined by whether or not the cycle counter is evenly divisible by the periodicity of each action. div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: Schedulability analysis can be divided into two stages. First, a timing model is built for the workload of each particular application. Second, this timing model is then submitted to a schedulability analysis algorithm to produce a timing report. The overall design is based on rate monotonic scheduling, and so it is a preemptive fixed priority workload description that is generated and analyzed.

div.head: Model Generation
div.p: The blocks of code that must be included in the timing model identified earlier are the scheduler construct, the port-to-port assignments and process dispatches within the scheduler construct, and the execution of the processes themselves.

The scheduler construct itself is modeled as the highest priority process executing at the highest rate. However, the port-to-port assignments and process dispatches are included as part of the associated process' compute time rather than the scheduler (where an assignment is associated with whichever connected process executes at the lowest rate). Since these scheduling actions actually occur non-preemptively when the scheduler executes, they must be modeled as blocking times for all processes of higher priority than the one with which they are associated. However, this produces more precise estimates of actual and breakdown utilization than simply including the largest block of scheduling actions in the scheduler process (taking the maximum compute time of the scheduler process over all CYCLE values).

From the user's perspective, the schedulability analysis algorithm we use allows process computation to be hierarchically decomposed into the compute times of a process' components. The set of components in each process consists of the scheduler actions associated with that process (which are also included as blocking components in all processes of higher priority), together with any components identified in the original MetaH specification (e.g. subl, sub2, foo in Figure 2). Among the latter may appear predeclared kernel service calls, which like scheduler actions are also included as blocking components in all processes of higher priority.

The compute times for the scheduler process template, kernel service calls, and process dispatches are given in the hardware architecture specification. The compute times for port-to-port assignments are estimated by a simple linear formula, A = C1 + Cz * B , where €3 is the number of bytes moved and Cl, C, are parameters recorded as attributes in the hardware architecture specification. Compute times for application source modules must be recorded in the MetaH specification, where the language supports a case expression that allows the time to be dependent on the type of processor t o which the containing process is ultimately bound. Compute times based on attribute values recorded in the hardware architecture specification are similarly conditioned on the final software/hardware binding.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: The analysis algorithm used is an extension of the exact characterization algorithm [6, 111. The schedulability analysis algorithm we use allows a process to be decomposed into a set of components, where the overall process compute time is the sum of the compute times of these components. The algorithm also produces sensitivity analysis values that show how much individual component or process compute times can be raised while maintaining schedule feasibility (or how much they must be lowered to achieve schedule feasibility).

Figure 6 shows the timing report produced from the specification in Figure 2. Summary figures for each process are shown on a line (e.g. RTSS93kerne1, P1, P2). Processes are listed in order of decreasing criticality (decreasing hardware priority, after necessary period transformations have been performed). The first process listed is always the scheduler process. Indented beneath each process appears a list of that process' components, where self is a component that represents source associated with the process entity itself and kernel is the scheduler action overhead attributed to that process.

The Budget times are those specified or estimated as described previously. The Critical times show how much the compute times of all processes and their components can simultaneously be raised while preserving feasibility. The Maximum times show how much the compute time of an individual process or component can be raised while preserving feasibility, providing all other processes and components stay within their budgeted compute times. The % Margin is the safety margin between the budgeted and the maximum compute time, the % Uti1 is the processor utilization devoted to that process or component, and Max Pri is the name of the highest priority process of which a component is a member (changing the compute time of a component will affect this and all lower priority processes).

We feel that allowing such a decomposition of processes into components, and the provision of sensitivity analysis information, is useful in practice. This supports an assessment of the risks associated with uncertainties in actual source module compute times and allows easy identification of bottlenecks or source modules on which to focus optimization efforts. For example, sub2 in Figure 6, with a relatively high utilization and low margin, represents a risk to the extent its compute time is uncertain, or a good candidate for further optimization. entities called modes and macros provide capabilities to specify system-level state transitions, similar to those of Statemate [5] and Durra. MetaH represents a selection, integration and extension of a variety of basic technologies in an attempt to meet the requirements of a range of avionics applications, with the objective being a transition of a number of advanced techniques and formal methods into practice. The MetaH tools have been used to develop, analyze and execute demonstrations of portions of a number of applications, including a flight management system and a missile controller. The MetaH system is part of a larger toolset designed to support the use of a multi-disciplinary, concurrent, architectureoriented development process for the production of GN&C software [l, 41.

We have described one particular aspect of the MetaH system, one that illustrates the basic technique of co-generation of timing models and executive code from the same specification in a way that (we hope) provides high assurance that the results of a schedulability analysis accurately capture the true real-time behavior of an application. Previous experiments have suggested this is possible in practice [12]. Periodic process and communication scheduling have more complex requirements in practice than indicated here, such as proper handling of process criticalities and preperiod deadlines when time is quantized by clock interrupt periodicity, scheduling and generation of fault-tolerant multi-processor communication protocol code, etc. Many other aspects that are important to provide in a system that is usable for a range of avionics applications, such as aperiodic processes, mode changes, event handling, faulttolerance, security, hardware architecture specification, etc., were omitted in the interest of brevity. MetaH provides features in all these areas, but these are also areas of current research and enhancement.
